preamble: Loss of laterality in Arabic ḍād ⟨ض⟩: the emphatic lateral of Classical Arabic, usually reconstructed as pharyngealized [ɮˤ] (or an affricate [dɮˤ]), became the emphatic stop [dˤ] of Modern Standard Arabic and of Egyptian, Levantine and Maghrebi dialects. Sibawayh described ḍād as articulated between the side of the tongue and the molars, and old loans keep a lateral: Spanish alcalde < al-qāḍī 'the judge', albayalde < bayāḍ 'white lead', arrabal and Old Leonese arraualde < rabaḍ 'suburb', Hausa alƙali, Akkadian ld or lṭ. Modern South Arabian cognates still have a lateral where Arabic has dˤ. Further back, the sound goes back to Proto-Semitic *ṣ́, reconstructed as an ejective lateral [ɬʼ] that survives in Modern South Arabian. Wiktionary describes the route as ɮˤ merging first with ẓāʾ [ðˤ] in speech and then becoming [dˤ] through stopping, with Qur'an readers later keeping dˤ for ḍād. The source is pharyngealized [ɮˤ], approximated here by plain [ɮ], and André Roman proposed [ʑˤ] instead, so the exact starting value is debated.
